landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet puts two small groups of cows, sheep and a hen on each row, with a plus sign between them and an empty box after the equals sign. Children count the animals in the first group, count the second group, and write how many there are altogether. A row might pair three cows with two more, or set a lone hen beside a pair of sheep, so the same skill returns with different pictures each time. The pictures carry the whole problem, so a child who cannot yet read an equation can still solve every row by touching and counting.
landings.p2: Counting two groups and then saying how many there are in all is the earliest form of addition. Long before the plus sign means anything, a child who can combine a pile of animals with another pile and recount the whole set is already adding. Keeping the totals within ten lets a kindergartner check the answer by counting rather than guessing.
landings.p3: On paper it makes a calm morning starter; on the board the whole class can count the herd together before anyone writes a number. When this set feels easy, take some animals away with subtraction, or count a different group in addition with vehicles. You can also browse every addition worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten. This is one of several animal addition sheets that work the same skill, so a class can return to it across the year.

landings.h1: Find the Missing Part — Animals — Kindergarten
landings.p1: On each row of this kindergarten worksheet a first group of animals is shown together with the total for the whole row, but the second group is an empty box. Children count the animals they can see, look at the total, and work out how many more belong in the box. Because both the part and the whole are pictured, a child can find the answer by counting up from what is there to the total, rather than by recalling a fact they have not learned yet.
landings.p2: Finding the part that is missing is how kindergartners first meet decomposition — the idea that a number like seven is made of smaller parts hiding inside it, such as five and two. It is the same thinking behind making ten, and it quietly prepares the ground for seeing how addition and subtraction fit together later on.
landings.p3: It is a gentle step up from straight counting, good for a small group who are ready for a little more thinking. When this feels easy, combine two full groups in addition with animals, or take some away in subtraction with animals. You can also browse every addition worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten. Each one prints for paper work or plays online with gentle, instant feedback.

landings.p1: Each row of this kindergarten worksheet shows a group of animals and asks the child to cross some of them out, then write how many are left. A row might start with five sheep and cross two away, or begin with a small herd and send one cow home, so the take-away looks different each time. The crossing-out is the heart of it: the child physically removes the animals that go away and counts the ones that remain, so subtraction is something they do with their hands before it becomes a written symbol.
landings.p2: Taking a few away and counting what is left is the most concrete form of subtraction there is, and it is exactly where five- and six-year-olds begin. Modelling the take-away with pictures they can cross out keeps the meaning — fewer than we started with — front and centre, well within ten so every answer can be checked by counting.
landings.p3: On the board it is a satisfying whole-class action; on paper it is a calm, hands-on task. When this feels easy, put groups together instead with addition with animals, or work out a missing part in find the missing part with animals. You can also browse every subtraction worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten. This is one of several animal subtraction sheets that practise the same skill.

landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet shows a scatter of animal pictures above an empty graph. The child sorts the animals by kind — all the cows together, all the sheep together — counts how many there are of each, and fills a column up to the matching height, building a simple picture graph one square at a time. The graph grows straight out of the child's own counting, so the bars mean something they made themselves rather than something handed to them.
landings.p2: Sorting things into groups and counting how many are in each is a genuine kindergarten skill, and showing those counts as a graph is the natural next step. The activity keeps both halves together — sort and count, then represent — so children see that a taller bar simply means there were more of that animal, not an abstract idea on a page.
landings.p3: It makes a strong shared lesson: build one column together on the board, then let children finish their own. When this feels easy, count and combine in addition with animals, or hunt for a letter in find and count with animals. You can also browse every picture graph worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten. Each graph prints on a single page or fills in on screen as children tap.

landings.h1: Find the Animals That Start with a Letter — Kindergarten
landings.p1: This kindergarten worksheet sets a target letter and fills a friendly scene with animals — some whose names begin with that letter, some that do not. The child finds and marks every animal whose name starts with the chosen letter, such as a cat, a cow and a camel for the letter C, then counts how many they found. Other animals are mixed in on purpose, so the child has to listen for the starting sound of each name rather than simply pointing at any picture.
landings.p2: Although it lives among the counting worksheets, the real work here is the link between a letter and the sound a word starts with — matching the printed letter to the first sound of each animal's name. That beginning-sound awareness is one of the first reading-readiness skills, and the counting at the end gives it a satisfying, low-pressure finish.
landings.p3: It works best chosen to match the letter a class is learning that week, so the hunt reinforces the lesson. When the hunt is done, count and combine in addition with animals, or make a graph in picture graph with animals. You can also browse every letter hunt worksheet or the whole animals collection for kindergarten.
